analysis.one_liner: Extends government funding into March while requiring documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote.
analysis.headline: The House defeated the package 202-220 on September 18, 2024, after 14 Republicans joined nearly all Democrats in opposition, and the Senate never voted on it.
analysis.plain_summary: This was a six-month stopgap funding bill to keep federal agencies open past October 1, 2024, at last year's spending levels, with $10 billion added for FEMA disaster relief and $1.95 billion for Virginia-class submarines. Republican leaders attached the SAVE Act, which would have barred states from processing a federal voter registration application unless the applicant showed documents proving U.S. citizenship, such as a passport, a compliant ID, or a certified birth certificate listing a parent's name. The House voted the combined package down, and a government shutdown was still pending when it failed.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone relying on federal programs kept running by the funding extension, including communities hit by disasters, which would get $10 billion for FEMA's relief fund [S2] [S3]. Homeowners in flood zones keep coverage through the National Flood Insurance Program extension [S2]. Defense shipbuilders gain $1.95 billion for Virginia-class submarines [S3]. Supporters of the voting provision say it ensures only citizens register; noncitizen voting is already illegal under existing law.

how_it_helps.text: Continues funding federal agencies at fiscal 2024 rates through the earlier of March 28, 2025 or passage of full-year bills, preventing a shutdown when fiscal 2025 began October 1, 2024 [S2].
Adds $10 billion to FEMA's Disaster Relief Fund for major declared disasters [S2] [S3].
Extends the National Flood Insurance Program and other expiring programs and authorities [S2].
Appropriates $1.95 billion for the Navy's Virginia-class submarine program [S3].
Requires every state to reject a federal voter registration application unless the applicant presents documentary proof of U.S. citizenship, with a defined list of acceptable documents [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Eligible citizens who lack a passport or a birth certificate meeting the bill's strict requirements would face a new hurdle to registering to vote, and states would have to build document-verification systems. The zeroed-out election security grants would remove $55 million states had otherwise received [S3]. The package also tied basic government funding to a contested voting rule, so its defeat left all of the funding provisions — including disaster aid — without a vehicle days before the shutdown deadline.
analysis.who_pays_short: Voters lacking citizenship documents; state election offices

drawbacks.text: The acceptable citizenship documents are a narrow list — a REAL ID Act ID showing citizenship, a passport, military ID with a service record, or a certified birth certificate listing a parent's full name [S3] — documents many eligible voters do not have on hand, which creates registration barriers for citizens who cannot readily produce them.
The bill sets Election Security Grants to $0, replacing the $55 million states otherwise receive [S3].

The stopgap simply freezes last year's spending for six months and defers all real budget decisions, while the addition of a partisan voting provision to must-pass funding created shutdown risk for services people depend on [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The funding half of the bill is routine: keep agencies open, add disaster relief, extend the flood insurance program. The serious trade-off is the SAVE Act rider, which addresses voting by noncitizens — already a federal crime — by imposing documentation requirements that fall hardest on eligible citizens who lack passports or matching birth certificates. Whether that trade was worth bundling into a shutdown-avoidance bill is exactly what the 202-220 floor vote decided, and voters' own representatives split almost entirely by party.

outcome.mechanism: The House debated it under a rule barring amendments, beat back a Democratic move to send it back to committee 209-214, then rejected the bill itself 202-220, and the Senate never took it up before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Republican leaders brought the bill to the floor under a closed rule allowing no amendments, with one hour of debate and one motion to recommit [S5].
Appropriations Ranking Member Rosa DeLauro moved to recommit the bill to committee; the motion failed 209-214, with all 209 voting Democrats in favor and all 214 voting Republicans opposed [S5] [S6].
Final passage failed 202-220 with 2 present: Democrats voted 3 for and 206 against, while Republicans voted 199 for and 14 against [S6].

Because it failed, the citizenship-proof voting requirement did not become law in the 118th Congress, and the bill's funding and disaster-relief provisions died with it, leaving Congress to fund the government another way before the October 1 deadline [S6] [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Opponents of the documentary-proof-of-citizenship voting requirement are better off because the bill failed and the requirement died with it, but the defeat also killed the bill's disaster relief and funding extensions, so Congress had to pass separate legislation to keep the government open.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Opponents of the citizenship proof requirement

for.name: Rep. Clay Higgins
for.what_they_did: Introduced the combined funding-and-SAVE Act bill with Rep. Cole on September 9, 2024 [S1] [S3].

for.name: Rep. Tom Cole
for.what_they_did: Co-introduced the bill and demanded the recorded vote on the motion to recommit [S3] [S5].

for.name: Speaker Mike Johnson
for.what_they_did: Announced and scheduled the strategy of attaching the SAVE Act to the stopgap funding bill, bringing it to the floor under a rule barring amendments.

against.name: 206 of 211 House Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage, rejecting the citizenship-documentation rider attached to government funding [S6].

against.name: Rep. Rosa DeLauro
against.what_they_did: Moved to recommit the bill to the Appropriations Committee, a move to strip the package back; the motion failed 209-214 [S5] [S6].

against.name: 14 of 220 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage, dooming the bill their party's leadership had brought to the floor [S6].

against.name: U.S. Senate
against.what_they_did: Never considered the bill after the House defeated it; no Senate action appears in the record [S1] [S5].

sides.party_line_note: Democrats opposed the package nearly unanimously (3 yeas, 206 nays of 211) while most Republicans backed it (199 yeas, 14 nays of 220), so the defeat rested on a nearly unified Democratic bloc plus 14 Republican defections.

industries.note: The bill carves out $1.95 billion for the Virginia-class submarine program on top of frozen fiscal-2024 funding, a direct win for the Navy's submarine builders [S3]. The cost flows through federal borrowing rather than an immediate charge to anyone.

The SAVE Act would require states to verify citizenship documents for every federal registration and build new checking systems, while the bill simultaneously cuts $55 million in election security grants to zero [S3]. Their added workload and lost funding track the reduced ease of registration for voters.

The stopgap locks in fiscal-2024 funding levels for nearly every agency through March 2025, keeping existing programs and contracts running unchanged [S2]. That preserves services people use but also freezes out any new priorities.
